text.title: Weighted Scoring Models
text.content: A weighted decision matrix compares options on criteria whose weights represent importance.

text.title: How to apply it
text.content: List the criteria and options, assign criterion weights, and score every option against each criterion using a consistent scale. Multiply each criterion score by its weight and add those products for the option’s total weighted score. Compare the totals to rank the options; the highest total is typically the best choice under the chosen criteria and weights.

text.title: A business analysis example
text.content:
Multiply each score by its criterion weight and add the products. A totals 4 × 0.6 + 2 × 0.4 = 3.2. B totals 3 × 0.6 + 4 × 0.4 = 3.4. B ranks higher under these chosen criteria, weights, and scores.

The highest total is typically the best choice under the chosen setup, not a universal fact that B is best in every context. The weights represent importance, and the scores express performance on the consistent scale. Record them so another reader can understand the comparison rather than seeing only the final total.

The practical output is an explicit weighted comparison of options. If a stakeholder challenges the recommendation, return to the criteria, importance weights, and scores. Do not defend 3.4 as if it were independent of those choices. The example weights sum to one; the key calculation is score times weight, summed across criteria.

text.title: Keep the distinction clear
text.content: Adding unweighted scores is not the weighted-total calculation. Multiply each criterion score by its importance weight first. Also keep the qualification: the highest total is typically best under the chosen criteria and weights, not proof of an objectively best solution in all circumstances.

notes: Preserve “typically”; do not prescribe weight normalization as mandatory.

text.content: Suppose stakeholders are choosing between two instruction-access solutions. Define shared criteria before comparing them: instruction clarity and fit with the agreed operating constraints. For this hypothetical assessment, use weights 0.6 and 0.4 and a common score scale.

text.title: Solution Option Evaluation and Recommendation
text.content: Solution comparison uses defined decision criteria rather than an unstructured preference.

text.title: How to apply it
text.content: Score each candidate solution against the same criteria and multiply the scores by the corresponding importance weights. Sum each candidate’s weighted scores, compare the totals, and explain the recommendation in terms of the criteria and scores.

text.title: A business analysis example
text.content:
Solution A scores 4 for clarity and 2 for fit, giving 4 × 0.6 + 2 × 0.4 = 3.2. Solution B scores 3 and 4, giving 3 × 0.6 + 4 × 0.4 = 3.4. Compare the totals and recommend B on this assessment, explaining that its stronger fit outweighs A’s clarity advantage under the selected weights.

The recommendation should point back to the criteria and scores. “We prefer B” omits the analytical basis; “B totals 3.4 under the agreed clarity and fit assessment” makes that basis visible. The two totals are hypothetical and depend on the chosen assessment, not a claim about real products.

The useful BA output is a reasoned solution recommendation, not only a completed matrix. State what was compared, how importance affected the scores, and how the resulting totals support the recommendation. Keep candidate solutions on the same criteria rather than awarding one option points for an advantage the other option was never assessed against.

text.title: Keep the distinction clear
text.content: A preferred option does not become a supported recommendation merely because it is given a score. Evaluate every candidate against the same criteria and weights, calculate the totals, and explain the recommendation in those terms rather than using an unstructured preference.

text.title: Business Case Development
text.content: A business case justifies an initiative by describing the problem, possible solutions, expected benefits, and costs.

text.title: How to apply it
text.content: List and estimate relevant costs and benefits over the period being evaluated, including direct and indirect effects. Present the recommendation with the supporting financial assessment in the business case. For a monetary-return estimate, calculate projected net return = total projected monetary benefits over the evaluation period − project cost, including the cost of the project itself rather than reporting gross savings alone. Interpret a positive projected monetary return as estimated benefits exceeding cost over that period, and report the assumptions and time horizon because the return is an estimate, not a promised financial outcome. Calculate percentage ROI = (monetary benefits − costs) / costs × 100%, using net monetary return as the numerator and investment cost as the denominator. Use the costs and monetary benefits for the stated evaluation period, include relevant costs rather than just a headline purchase cost, and use the same time period when comparing alternatives. Net monetary return is the benefits-minus-costs amount in money, whereas percentage ROI expresses that net return relative to investment cost.

text.title: A business analysis example
text.content:
Projected net monetary return is benefits minus costs: 18,000 − 12,000 = 6,000. Percentage ROI is that net return divided by investment cost, times 100%: 6,000 / 12,000 × 100% = 50%. The 6,000 amount and 50% percentage describe different things. Gross benefits of 18,000 are not the net return.

A positive projected monetary return means the estimated benefits exceed cost over the stated period. Report the one-year horizon and the assumptions behind the estimates; this is not a promised financial outcome. If another alternative is compared, use costs and monetary benefits for the same evaluation period, including relevant direct and indirect effects.

Present the recommendation with its supporting financial assessment in the business case. Do not let the calculation replace the problem and option descriptions. The useful output explains why the initiative is being considered and what estimated return supports the recommendation, with the costs, period, and assumptions visible to readers.

text.title: Keep the distinction clear
text.content: ROI’s numerator is net monetary return, not gross savings. Its denominator is investment cost, not benefits. A positive projection is an estimate under stated assumptions and a time horizon, not a promise. Net return in money and percentage ROI must not be labeled interchangeably.

text.content: Suppose two instruction-access options differ in cost and clarity. Cost is measured in money, while clarity uses a rating. Adding 8,000 directly to a clarity score of 4 would mix incompatible units, so define a common rating scale first.

text.title: Multi-Criteria Decision Analysis
text.content: A decision matrix enables comparison across several criteria using explicit importance weights and scores.

text.title: How to apply it
text.content: Define criteria and importance weights, then map each criterion’s performance values to a common rating scale with criterion-specific scoring definitions applied consistently to all options and higher ratings meaning better performance. Calculate each option’s total by multiplying its common-scale rating for each criterion by that criterion’s weight and summing these weighted ratings, rather than raw values in incompatible units, then compare totals for a defensible ranking.

text.title: A business analysis example
text.content:
For this hypothetical matrix, clarity already uses 1 to 5, with higher ratings better. Define cost ratings specifically: 8,000 maps to 5 and 12,000 maps to 3 for the example options, because lower cost is better under the chosen scoring definitions. Apply each criterion’s definition consistently to every option. Assign weights 0.4 to cost and 0.6 to clarity.

Option A has cost rating 5 and clarity 3, totaling 5 × 0.4 + 3 × 0.6 = 3.8. Option B has cost rating 3 and clarity 5, totaling 3 × 0.4 + 5 × 0.6 = 4.2. Compare those totals for the ranking.

The useful output makes criteria, importance, criterion-specific scoring definitions, and weighted totals explicit. The invented mappings are part of this assessment, not a universal monetary conversion. Higher ratings must mean better performance across the criteria, including cost, so the weighted sum has a consistent interpretation.

text.title: Keep the distinction clear
text.content: Weights do not make incompatible raw units directly comparable. Map performance to a common rating scale with criterion-specific definitions first. Also reverse the scoring direction where needed so higher ratings mean better performance rather than accidentally rewarding higher cost.

required_facts.statement: The sample mean is computed as the sum of the observed values divided by the number of observations.
The median is the middle value when the data are ordered from smallest to largest; if there is an even number of observations, the median is the average of the two middle values.
The mode is the value that occurs most often in the data; there can be more than one mode.

The mean is more strongly affected by extreme observations (such as those in the tail of a skewed distribution) than the median, which is more robust to them; for this reason the median can better represent a typical value in a skewed dataset.

optional_enrichment.statement: A mode is a prominent peak in a distribution: a value or narrow range of values where observations are noticeably more concentrated than in neighboring regions.

text.content: Imagine five observed dispatch-preparation times in minutes: 2, 3, 3, 4, and 18. The mean is the sum divided by the number of observations: 30 / 5 = 6 minutes. The ordered middle value is 3, so the median is 3 minutes. The most frequent value is also 3, so the mode is 3 minutes.

text.title: Descriptive Measures Of Center
text.content: The sample mean is computed as the sum of the observed values divided by the number of observations.

text.title: How to apply it
text.content: The median is the middle value when the data are ordered from smallest to largest; if there is an even number of observations, the median is the average of the two middle values. The mode is the value that occurs most often in the data; there can be more than one mode. The mean is more strongly affected by extreme observations (such as those in the tail of a skewed distribution) than the median, which is more robust to them; for this reason the median can better represent a typical value in a skewed dataset.

text.title: A business analysis example
text.content:
The extreme 18-minute observation affects the mean more strongly than the median. In this skewed sample, the median can better represent a typical value than the mean. Do not hide the extreme observation; explain why the two center summaries differ.

For an even-sized example, 2, 3, 4, and 9 has median (3 + 4) / 2 = 3.5. For mode, 2, 2, 4, and 4 has two most frequent values, so both 2 and 4 are modes. These examples apply the definitions rather than assuming every dataset has a single mode or a median that is an observed value.

The practical BA task is to interpret a center measure in the context of the business data. A report saying “average preparation time is 6 minutes” should be clear that it uses the mean. The median answers a different center question and is more robust to extreme observations.

text.title: Keep the distinction clear
text.content: Mean, median, and mode are not interchangeable names for one number. Order values before finding the median, average the two middle values when the count is even, and allow multiple modes. An extreme value can pull the mean away from the median.

practice_anchor.objective: Order the hypothetical dispatch-preparation times 2, 3, 3, 4, and 18 minutes; compute their mean, median, and mode using arithmetic; and justify which best represents a typical preparation time. required_facts.statement: The range of a data set is the largest value minus the smallest value.

The variance is computed by taking each observation's deviation from the mean, squaring it, summing the squared deviations, and dividing by n - 1 (one less than the number of observations); it is roughly the average squared distance of the observations from the mean.
The standard deviation is the square root of the variance, and it describes the typical distance of an observation from the mean.

The standard deviation is expressed in the same units as the original data, while the variance is expressed in squared units; the range is based only on the two most extreme values and ignores how the rest of the data are spread.

text.content: Suppose dispatch-preparation times are 2, 4, and 6 minutes. Their mean is 4. The range is 6 − 2 = 4 minutes. For the sample variance, subtract the mean from each observation to get -2, 0, and 2; square these deviations to get 4, 0, and 4; then sum to 8.

text.title: Measures Of Spread
text.content: The range of a data set is the largest value minus the smallest value.

text.title: How to apply it
text.content: The variance is computed by taking each observation's deviation from the mean, squaring it, summing the squared deviations, and dividing by n - 1 (one less than the number of observations); it is roughly the average squared distance of the observations from the mean. The standard deviation is the square root of the variance, and it describes the typical distance of an observation from the mean. The standard deviation is expressed in the same units as the original data, while the variance is expressed in squared units; the range is based only on the two most extreme values and ignores how the rest of the data are spread.

text.title: A business analysis example
text.content:
Divide by n − 1, which is 2 for three observations: variance is 8 / 2 = 4 square minutes. Standard deviation is the square root of that variance, or 2 minutes. The different units matter: variance is squared, while standard deviation uses the original minutes and describes typical distance from the mean.

Range only uses the smallest and largest values. A second sample, 2, 4, 4, 4, and 6, has the same range, but its variance is 8 / 4 = 2 square minutes and standard deviation is about 1.41 minutes. The added central observations change the spread calculation without changing the extremes.

The practical reporting point is that range alone does not describe how the rest of the data are spread. State which measure you use and its units. The variance formula here is the sample form with n − 1; keep that denominator instead of silently switching to another convention.

text.title: Keep the distinction clear
text.content: Do not divide this sample-variance calculation by n: the stated denominator is n − 1. Standard deviation is not the variance itself, and it is not in squared units. Equal ranges also do not prove equal spread among all observations.

practice_anchor.objective: Use arithmetic to compute the range, sample variance, and standard deviation for dispatch-preparation times of 2, 4, and 6 minutes, then compare their consistency with times of 2, 4, 4, 4, and 6 minutes.

Explain that both means are 4 minutes, but the second sample has less spread around the mean and is more consistent despite the equal ranges.

required_facts.statement: A user story states a persona’s need and its purpose using “As a [persona], I [want to], [so that].”
Refine oversized backlog items by breaking them into smaller, more precise items with clearer descriptions.
Split larger stories into smaller stories that can be completed within an iteration.
Use INVEST as a quality checklist for each rewritten or split story; if a criterion fails, consider rewording or rewriting the story.
Independent means stories should not overlap in concept and should be schedulable and implementable in any order; check whether a story can be implemented without requiring another story first.
Negotiable means a story captures the essential need rather than a fixed contract of feature details; check that details can be worked out collaboratively with the customer.
Valuable means a story delivers value to the customer; check that each split story describes a customer-valued result rather than only a technical layer.
Estimable means the team can approximate the work well enough to rank and schedule it; check that the team understands the story and its scope well enough to make an estimate.
Small means a story fits within an iteration; check the size of each proposed story and split work that cannot fit.
Testable means the desired result is clear enough to write a test for it; check that the customer can describe how to verify the story, and clarify stories whose result cannot be tested.

text.content: Imagine a backlog story saying, “As a dispatcher, I want all order-management capabilities, so that I can do my work.” It is broad enough that the team cannot clearly discuss its scope or finish it within an iteration. Refinement breaks oversized items into smaller, more precise stories.

text.title: User Story Writing and Refinement
text.content: A user story states a persona’s need and its purpose using “As a [persona], I [want to], [so that].”

text.title: How to apply it
text.content: Refine oversized backlog items by breaking them into smaller, more precise items with clearer descriptions. Split larger stories into smaller stories that can be completed within an iteration. Use INVEST as a quality checklist for each rewritten or split story; if a criterion fails, consider rewording or rewriting the story. Independent means stories should not overlap in concept and should be schedulable and implementable in any order; check whether a story can be implemented without requiring another story first. Negotiable means a story captures the essential need rather than a fixed contract of feature details; check that details can be worked out collaboratively with the customer. Valuable means a story delivers value to the customer; check that each split story describes a customer-valued result rather than only a technical layer. Estimable means the team can approximate the work well enough to rank and schedule it; check that the team understands the story and its scope well enough to make an estimate. Small means a story fits within an iteration; check the size of each proposed story and split work that cannot fit. Testable means the desired result is clear enough to write a test for it; check that the customer can describe how to verify the story, and clarify stories whose result cannot be tested.

text.title: A business analysis example
text.content:
For this hypothetical case, rewrite one story around seeing current instructions and another around finding orders by customer. Each needs a persona’s need and purpose, not merely a technical layer. Check each rewritten story with INVEST. Independent asks whether it can be implemented without requiring the other first and without conceptual overlap. Negotiable asks whether it captures the essential need while details remain open to collaboration. Valuable asks whether it delivers a customer-valued result.

Estimable asks whether the team understands it well enough to approximate the work for ranking and scheduling. Small asks whether it fits within an iteration. Testable asks whether the customer can describe how to verify the result. If the rewritten instruction story still says only “make access better,” clarify it until a test can be described. If it cannot fit, split it further.

The output is not just more story cards. It is a set of clearer, smaller stories checked for all six qualities. The example split is a candidate to assess, not a guarantee of independence or size without the team’s checks.

text.title: Keep the distinction clear
text.content: Splitting into “database,” “interface,” and “testing” pieces does not by itself satisfy Valuable: each split story should describe a customer-valued result. Nor does using the story sentence format prove INVEST is met. Check each quality and reword or rewrite failures.

practice_anchor.objective: Split the oversized dispatcher story about all order-management capabilities into two or three smaller stories, using the hypothetical needs of seeing current instructions and finding orders by customer. Write each in the persona–need–purpose format and assess each against all six INVEST criteria.
practice_anchor.success: Submit two or three precise stories, each expressing a persona, need, and customer-valued purpose, together with an INVEST check for each. Check conceptual overlap and whether either story requires another first; keep details negotiable; explain customer value, scope clarity for estimation, iteration fit, and how the customer could verify the result. Reword or split any identified failures, and identify assumptions needing team or customer confirmation rather than declaring independence or iteration fit without support.

visual_anchor.purpose: Show the oversized dispatcher story alongside two or three candidate smaller stories. Annotate each candidate's persona, need, and purpose, and display the six INVEST checks, distinguishing supported qualities from assumptions that still require confirmation.

notes: Include all INVEST meanings; do not assume an invented split is automatically independent.
Use the supplied hypothetical business situation; do not treat its policies, numbers, or outcomes as universal rules.

required_facts.statement: A product backlog is an emergent, ordered list of work needed to improve the product.
Refinement breaks items into smaller, more precise items and adds details such as description, order, and size.
Review unclear or oversized items, clarify their details, split them as needed, and keep the backlog ordered.
Items that can be completed within one iteration are ready for selection; refinement usually provides the needed transparency.

text.content: Suppose the order-service backlog contains a broad instruction-access item, a clearer customer-search item, and an outdated vague item called “reporting improvements.” The product backlog is an emergent ordered list of needed product-improvement work, not a fixed archive of every initial idea.

text.title: Backlog Management
text.content: A product backlog is an emergent, ordered list of work needed to improve the product.

text.title: How to apply it
text.content: Refinement breaks items into smaller, more precise items and adds details such as description, order, and size. Review unclear or oversized items, clarify their details, split them as needed, and keep the backlog ordered. Items that can be completed within one iteration are ready for selection; refinement usually provides the needed transparency.

text.title: A business analysis example
text.content:
Refine unclear or oversized items. For the instruction item, clarify the description and break it into smaller, more precise items if needed. For the vague reporting item, establish the intended detail before treating it as ready. Add detail such as description, order, and size, then keep the backlog ordered.

Items that can be completed within one iteration are ready for selection; refinement usually provides the transparency needed for that judgment. Do not label an oversized item ready merely because it appears near the top. Conversely, refinement is not just changing order: it also improves detail and precision.

The useful BA contribution is clearer items and an understandable ordered backlog. Keep clarification, splitting, detail, and ordering visible rather than treating the backlog as a static archive.

text.title: Keep the distinction clear
text.content: A backlog is not simply an unordered requirements list. Refinement also does more than re-rank items: it makes them smaller and more precise with relevant details. High placement alone does not establish that an item fits within an iteration.

practice_anchor.objective: Refine a messy order-service backlog containing instruction access, customer search, and reporting improvements. Use supplied business priorities and clarification details to reorder items, split oversized work into smaller precise items, add description and size details, and mark refinement status.
practice_anchor.success: The backlog reflects the supplied priorities; unclear items have clarified descriptions or remain marked as needing clarification; oversized items are split as needed; and only sufficiently clear items that can be completed within one iteration are marked ready for selection.

visual_anchor.purpose: Show the order-service backlog before and after refinement, making changes to item order, descriptions, size, splitting, and refinement status visible. Distinguish high placement from readiness for selection.

notes: Preserve “usually” for refinement transparency; avoid assigning later Scrum accountabilities prematurely.
Use the supplied hypothetical business situation; do not treat its policies, numbers, or outcomes as universal rules.

required_facts.statement: A roadmap sequences planned work against goals rather than listing disconnected features.
Group planned initiatives into a sequence such as Now, Next, and Later, linking the sequence to goals and tracking dependencies.
source_refs: atlassian_agile#https://www.atlassian.com/agile/product-management/roadmaps — Who is responsible for the product roadmap?; roadmap examples; Tips and tricks

required_facts.statement: Review the sequence as priorities and information change rather than treating the initial roadmap as fixed.

text.content: Imagine planned order-service work includes current-instruction access, a customer-search improvement, and broader multi-branch reporting. A roadmap sequences planned work against goals rather than presenting disconnected features.

text.title: Phased Delivery Sequencing
text.content: A roadmap sequences planned work against goals rather than listing disconnected features.

text.title: How to apply it
text.content: Group planned initiatives into a sequence such as Now, Next, and Later, linking the sequence to goals and tracking dependencies. Review the sequence as priorities and information change rather than treating the initial roadmap as fixed.

text.title: A business analysis example
text.content:
For this hypothetical roadmap, place instruction access in Now to support the dispatch-preparation goal, customer search in Next to support faster order finding, and multi-branch reporting in Later to support branch comparison. Track known dependencies as part of the sequence. If later reporting depends on agreed branch information, make that connection visible instead of treating the three labels as independent wish lists.

Now, Next, and Later are an example sequence, not fixed dates promised by this concept. Link each initiative to its goal so a stakeholder can understand why it occupies that part of the roadmap. Then review the sequence as priorities and information change.

If new information changes which work supports the immediate goal, reconsider the initial placement. The useful output is goal-linked planned sequencing with dependencies and revision, not a permanent commitment disguised as a diagram. The example initiatives are invented for the exercise; their particular order is not a universal rule for BA delivery.

text.title: Keep the distinction clear
text.content: A roadmap is not just a list of features with three headings. The sequence should connect to goals and track dependencies. Also, the initial sequence is not fixed: review it as priorities and information change rather than claiming the first roadmap cannot be revised.

practice_anchor.objective: Sequence 10 prioritized requirements from the hypothetical order-service situation into three releases, using supplied goals and dependencies to justify their placement.
practice_anchor.success: All 10 requirements are assigned to three goal-linked releases. Each prerequisite is placed before the work that depends on it, including an explicit internal order if both share a release. Placement reflects the supplied priorities without treating release labels as fixed dates.

visual_anchor.purpose: Make the three-release sequence visible, with all 10 requirements grouped by release, each release linked to its goal, and dependency arrows showing prerequisite order.

media.group_title: Goal-linked releases that change with learning

segments.label: Sequence releases around goals and revise them as information changes
segments.summary: An online bookstore example groups planned work into releases with different goals. The first release supports validation through a basic end-to-end flow: a home page, title search, adding a book to a shopping cart, and credit-card checkout. A second release aims toward public availability by adding categories, book details, and removal from the cart. If learning shows that customers will not pay by credit card, cash on delivery moves into the second release. Other additions are deferred: further stakeholder-requested features are considered for release three, while PayPal checkout and buying multiple copies of a book are considered for release four. These placements illustrate a sequence that changes with new information, not a universal release plan.

bridge_note.before: Watch how the bookstore example links releases to validation and public availability, then changes the sequence when payment preferences become clearer. Its numbered releases illustrate sequencing rather than fixed dates.
bridge_note.after: The clip illustrates goal-linked sequencing and revision. It does not fully teach grouping initiatives into Now, Next, and Later with explicit dependency tracking; the text covers that missing element.

notes: Do not invent scheduling authority or fixed durations for Now/Next/Later.
Use the supplied hypothetical business situation; do not treat its policies, numbers, or outcomes as universal rules.

required_facts.statement: Acceptance criteria state the conditions used to determine whether a particular user story is satisfied.
Discuss what completing the story means, make the acceptance conditions testable, and document that shared understanding.
source_refs: atlassian_user_stories#https://www.atlassian.com/agile/project-management/user-stories — How to write user stories — Definition of done; What is in a user story?

required_facts.statement: Refinement adds detail to make backlog items more precise and understandable.

text.content: Suppose a story says dispatchers want to see current instructions so they can prepare the correct order. Acceptance criteria state the conditions used to judge whether this particular story is satisfied. Discuss what completing it means instead of relying only on the story’s short wording.

text.title: Acceptance Criteria Definition
text.content: Acceptance criteria state the conditions used to determine whether a particular user story is satisfied.

text.title: How to apply it
text.content: Discuss what completing the story means, make the acceptance conditions testable, and document that shared understanding. Refinement adds detail to make backlog items more precise and understandable.

text.title: A business analysis example
text.content:
For this hypothetical case, the stakeholders agree that selecting an existing order displays its current instructions, and selecting an unknown identifier displays a not-found result. Make those acceptance conditions testable and document the shared understanding. “The lookup is good” does not describe a clear completion condition.

During refinement, add detail that makes the backlog item more precise and understandable. If stakeholders disagree about what “current” means, clarify that point before leaving the criterion as if everyone interpreted it identically. The example conditions are agreed choices for this story, not a complete checklist for all instruction-access systems.

The useful output is story-specific completion understanding that can be checked. It should connect directly to the desired behavior rather than becoming a broad quality slogan. Keep the conditions in the shared record so later discussion is about the documented understanding, not a different person’s recollection of what was meant.

text.title: Keep the distinction clear
text.content: Acceptance criteria belong to a particular story. They are not a substitute for clarifying what that story means, and vague positive wording does not make them testable. Discuss and document the shared completion conditions instead of assuming the title is sufficient.

practice_anchor.objective: Facilitate a mock refinement discussion for the dispatcher instruction-access story. Clarify what completing the story means, resolve differing interpretations of “current,” and document agreed, testable conditions for an existing order and an unknown identifier.
practice_anchor.success: The shared record contains story-specific conditions with observable results for both cases, an agreed meaning of “current,” and confirmation that the participants share the documented understanding. The refined item is more precise and understandable, without vague conditions such as “the lookup is good.”

visual_anchor.purpose: Show the dispatcher story alongside a vague condition and the agreed, testable conditions for existing and unknown order identifiers. Annotate the clarified meaning of “current” and the observable result for each condition.

notes: Do not introduce Definition of Done early; focus on testable story conditions.
Use the supplied hypothetical business situation; do not treat its policies, numbers, or outcomes as universal rules.
